title: The Jedburgh and the Family Jewels: from a drop zone in the Yonne to a canoe on the Wicomico
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: St. Paul, Minnesota, the birth between two postings
stops.date_confidence: attested: 4 January 1920 (Britannica, Wikipedia). No hospital, ward, or parish is named in any reachable source.
stops.campa: A son is born in St. Paul to Elbridge Colby, an English professor who has taken an Army commission, and to Margaret Mary Egan, whose family runs deep in the city's Democratic politics. He is the only child of the marriage. The birth falls between two of his father's postings, and the uniform will set his geography for the next twenty years. Nothing survives of the day but the city name, which every obituary he ever gets will repeat. He will not live here again.
suggested_refs: St. Paul, Minnesota, birthplace named in every Colby obituary and biographical summary

stops.name: Panama City, the Canal Zone garrison
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: biographers name Panama among the father's postings without giving a fort or a year, so the date is a placeholder inside the 1920s. The pin is the atlas's canonical Panama City coordinate, inherited from the Noriega file, not a located garrison.
stops.campa: The infant is carried to a Canal Zone garrison as his father rotates through Army posts. Biographers name Panama beside China and the American mainland among the stations of the early childhood, and specify neither fort nor year. The heat and the segregated Zone towns leave no mark in anything he later writes. Thirty-two years on, a Panamanian officer named Manuel Noriega goes onto the CIA payroll and stays there through every directorship including Colby's own.
suggested_refs: The Panama Canal Zone garrisons of the 1920s, one of the postings of Elbridge Colby's Army career

stops.name: Tianjin, the treaty port
stops.date_confidence: residence attested (Wikipedia's William Colby article lists Tianjin among the childhood postings; Encyclopedia.com says China). The years c. 1927-1929 and the 'military and academic post' are unsupported: there is no Wikipedia article on Elbridge Colby the professor-soldier, only one on his great-grandson. Year defaulted to the middle of the claimed span.
stops.campa: His father's postings carry the family to Tianjin, into the foreign concessions of a treaty port thick with gunboats and Kuomintang unrest. The boy is seven or eight. Decades later he will run the CIA's Far East Division and its Saigon station and will draw nothing specific from this address in anything he writes. The record places him here and gives neither an address nor a date of departure. What the concessions taught him, if they taught him anything, he never said.
suggested_refs: The foreign concessions of Tianjin in the late 1920s, where the family followed Elbridge Colby's posting

stops.name: Burlington, Vermont, the settled years
stops.date_confidence: attested in biographical summary (Britannica; Princeton Alumni Weekly memorial) to the mid-1930s; no year of entry or graduation is given, and the date is set at the middle of the span.
stops.campa: After the postings abroad the family settles in Burlington, and Colby finishes growing up in a Vermont public high school while his father teaches nearby. It is the first stable stretch of his boyhood and the last one for a long time. The years leave almost no documentary trace beyond the bare fact of attendance. What the town supplies is the ordinary American adolescence that a career run out of Stockholm, Rome, and Saigon otherwise lacks. He keeps ties to the state for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: Burlington High School, Vermont, the only settled schooling of Colby's childhood
sources: Princeton Alumni Weekly, 'William E. Colby '40' memorial

stops.name: Princeton, the class of 1940
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of the degree (Britannica; Wikipedia); the graduation day is not given and June is the conventional default. That he edited the college newspaper rests on one memorial notice and is carried as reconstruction.
stops.campa: He enters Princeton and takes his A.B. in politics in 1940, writing his senior thesis on the Spanish Civil War while Europe collapses and American isolationism curdles into alarm. The class is one that will send an unusual number of its men into the Office of Strategic Services and then into the Central Intelligence Agency. The campus is gothic and sure of itself. Colby, whose household was never patrician, spends four years among the sons of the eastern establishment he will be surrounded by for the rest of his working life.
suggested_refs: Colby's 1940 Princeton senior thesis on the Spanish Civil War

stops.name: Columbia Law School, the degree the war interrupts
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1941 (Wikipedia); the month is not recorded and is set to the start of the academic year.
stops.campa: He enters Columbia Law School and volunteers for the Army as the war closes in, and he will not finish the degree until 1947. The gap between matriculation and diploma is the war itself, folded invisibly into one line of a resume. When he comes back to Morningside Heights he is carrying a Silver Star, decorations from Norway, France, and Britain, and a working fluency in demolition and clandestine organization that no course in the building teaches.
suggested_refs: Columbia Law School matriculation records for 1941 and the conferral of Colby's LL.B. in 1947

stops.name: Fort Benning, Georgia, the parachute wings
stops.date_confidence: weak. The paratrooper qualification is attested in every account of his war, but Fort Benning as the site and 1943 as the year rest on a single source, warhistory.org, which returned HTTP 403 in this pass. Month unknown and defaulted. The pin is the Airborne School main post area; the coordinates circulating in the research pool fell in the city of Columbus, off the installation.
stops.campa: He earns his parachute wings at the Army jump school: towers, and the count of four before the canopy opens. Every account of his war names him a paratrooper before it names him anything else, and the qualification is what lets the Office of Strategic Services drop him twice into occupied Europe. The training is brutal and ordinary, thousands of men doing the same thing in the same season without knowing what any of them are being sorted for. It is welded on months before Normandy and a full year before Norway.
suggested_refs: The U.S. Army Airborne School at Fort Benning, standard pipeline for OSS operational personnel
sources: WarHistory.org, 'William E. Colby' (cited in the research pool; HTTP 403 on retrieval)
General OSS histories of the Jedburgh selection pipeline

stops.name: Milton Hall, Peterborough, the Jedburgh school
stops.date_confidence: attested to the season. The estate hosted the Jedburgh school from 1943 and trained 93 teams and 276 personnel; Colby's own course was the 1944 intake preceding his August drop, not the 1943 one the research pool implied. Coordinates corrected to 52 deg 35 min 04 sec N, 0 deg 18 min 42 sec W.
stops.campa: At Milton Hall, a country estate three miles east of Peterborough requisitioned as the joint OSS and SOE finishing school, Colby trains for the Jedburghs: three-man teams built to arm and organize the French resistance ahead of the invasion. Ninety-three teams pass through the house. He is matched with a French officer and a radio operator under the team name Bruce. The syllabus covers demolitions, unarmed killing, and the etiquette of parachuting into a country under occupation. The motto handed down the program is surprise, kill, and vanish.
suggested_refs: Milton Hall, Cambridgeshire, the joint OSS-SOE Jedburgh finishing school, 1943-1944

stops.name: The Yonne, France, the drop of Team Bruce
stops.date_confidence: attested: the night of 13 into 14 August 1944 (CENTCOM Citadel; European Center of Military History). The coordinate is a departmental centroid; the exact drop zone is not given in any reachable source. The research pool's claim that the sector was liberated in the second week of September conflicts with the record, Sens falling 21 August and Auxerre 24 August.
stops.campa: On the night of the thirteenth of August, Team Bruce jumps from a blacked-out Carpetbagger B-24 into the Yonne, southeast of Paris. The pilot misjudges the run and puts them down some twenty miles from the intended field, on German-held ground rather than beside the waiting maquis. Thunderstorms turn the fields to mud that same night. For the rest of the month they cut German communications and arm resistance units, and by the last week of August the towns of the department, Sens and then Auxerre, are free.
suggested_refs: Jedburgh Team BRUCE operational reports, Yonne, August to September 1944
sources: CENTCOM Citadel, 'Jedburgh teams behind enemy lines'
European Center of Military History, 'Jedburgh 12 AG Support 1944'

stops.name: Jaevsjoen, Norway, the ice at the opening of Operation Rype
stops.date_confidence: attested: 24 March 1945. Coordinates from Wikidata Q6977515 for the lake straddling Snaasa and Aare; the figures circulating in the research pool pointed at Snaasa village, some 40 km northwest. Personnel counts conflict: 35 designed and 15 arrived (HistoryNet) against 31 expected and 12 arrived (secondary summaries). The journey follows the traceable figures.
stops.campa: Colby and his companions drop onto the ice of a frozen mountain lake on the Norwegian-Swedish border, the opening jump of Operation Rype. Thirty-five men are meant to be on that ice. Three of the B-24s never find the lake and turn back for Scotland, one puts five men down in neutral Sweden who will come on later by foot, and fifteen arrive. The cold is absolute and the ice holds. It is the only combined ski and parachute operation the United States Army mounts in the war.
suggested_refs: Lake Jaevsjoen, drop zone of Operation Rype, 24 March 1945

stops.name: Gjefsjoen, the mountain farm as headquarters
stops.date_confidence: attested to the spring of 1945; the day of occupation is not recorded and is set two days after the drop. Coordinates published by the farm itself, 64 deg 06 min 16 sec N, 13 deg 05 min 05 sec E; the research pool's figures again pointed at Snaasa village.
stops.campa: The team makes its headquarters at an isolated mountain farm above the lake, thirty kilometers from the nearest road, supplied by Norwegians who risk reprisal to feed and shelter them. Skis do the work of vehicles. The owners of the farm become unpaid partisans. The building still stands and tells this winter to its visitors: American irregulars bunked in a hayloft, waiting on weather and on the men the drop scattered across two countries. The railway they came for runs through the valleys to the west.
suggested_refs: Gjefsjoen Fjellgaard, Snaasa, operational base of the NORSO Group in spring 1945

stops.name: The Grana bridge, the target that is left standing
stops.date_confidence: the decision is attested (HistoryNet; The Norwegian American) but undated; April is inferred from the operational sequence and the day defaulted. Coordinates approximate, consistent with HistoryNet's 'twenty-four miles west of camp' but given by no source directly.
stops.campa: The Grana bridge on the Nordland line is Rype's assigned target, the structure whose loss would sever the railway the Germans need to pull their divisions out of the far north before the Soviets cut them off. It is heavily guarded and lies twenty-four miles west of the farm. Colby, with a fraction of his team on the ground, decides against it. The war in Norway is fought instead against smaller structures that a handful of men on skis can reach and leave.
suggested_refs: The Grana bridge on the Nordlandsbanen, Rype's assigned primary target, never attacked
sources: The Norwegian American, on the Rype demolitions

stops.name: Tangen, the bridge that goes down instead
stops.date_confidence: attested: about 06:30 on 15 April 1945 (gjefsjo.no); HistoryNet gives 14-15 April. Coordinates approximate, given by no source. The research pool's claim that the party was reinforced by Operation Woodlark personnel is unsupported by any source checked.
stops.campa: At about half past six in the morning, Lieutenant Glen Farnsworth and three Norwegians blow the bridge at Tangen south of Snaasa: four steel I-beams, thirty-six feet each, over a creek thirteen feet wide. It is not the Grana. It is the railway all the same, and the line goes down. German patrols work the district constantly, and the party skis out rather than holding ground, which is the doctrine Milton Hall taught and the reason the Jedburgh teams were built small.
suggested_refs: The Tangen railway bridge south of Snaasa, demolished 15 April 1945

stops.name: Lurudalen, two and a half kilometers of track
stops.date_confidence: attested: 23 April 1945 (HistoryNet). Coordinates approximate; the valley is named in the sources but no demolition point is given.
stops.campa: On the twenty-third of April the team destroys two and a half kilometers of track in the Lurudalen valley, the last major demolition of the campaign. It is not a strike on a structure but an erasure of usable rail. Within three weeks Germany surrenders and the war in Norway ends, and the men who spent a winter on skis in an occupied country stand down and scatter into peacetime. Most of them will not spend their lives in intelligence work. Colby is decorated by his own government and by three others.
suggested_refs: The Lurudalen track demolition of 23 April 1945, the last major action of Operation Rype
sources: WarHistory.org, 'William E. Colby' (decorations; HTTP 403 on retrieval)

segments.name: The Law Office and the First Stations

stops.name: New York, the firm of the old OSS chief
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year the LL.B. was conferred (Encyclopedia.com); month defaulted. The firm's 1947 name was Donovan, Leisure, Newton, Lombard and Irvine. The move on to the National Labor Relations Board came at the end of the stint, about 1949, not at its start as the research pool had it.
stops.campa: Degree finally in hand, Colby practices for two years at the downtown firm founded by his old OSS chief. The move is less a career choice than a continuation of loyalty by other means: Wild Bill Donovan's wartime network reconstitutes itself as a law office while its members wait to see whether Washington will stand up a permanent peacetime intelligence service. It does, in 1947, the same year the diploma is conferred. Colby leaves at the end of the decade for the National Labor Relations Board and a Washington address.
suggested_refs: Donovan, Leisure, Newton, Lombard and Irvine, the postwar reconstitution of the OSS network as a law firm

stops.name: The E Street complex, Washington, joining the agency
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1950 (Britannica, Wikipedia); month unrecorded and defaulted. Pin corrected to the E Street Complex at 2430 E Street NW, the CIA's headquarters until the 1961 move to Langley; the coordinates in the research pool fell in Adams Morgan and matched no agency facility of any period.
stops.campa: Colby joins the Central Intelligence Agency in Foggy Bottom, eleven years before the agency moves to Langley. Korea has just opened, the early Cold War bureaucracy is hardening, and the place is still young enough to be improvising its own procedures, staffed heavily by men who already know each other from occupied Europe. He is processed and trained and sent abroad within the year. The generation that jumped into France has become the generation that runs the stations.
suggested_refs: The CIA's E Street Complex, 2430 E Street NW, headquarters from 1947 until the 1961 move to Langley

stops.name: Stockholm, the stay-behind networks
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1951-1953 (Britannica, Wikipedia); no month given, defaulted. Everything beyond the fact of the posting is reconstruction: no specific operation from this station appears in any open biography.
stops.campa: His first posting abroad puts him under embassy cover in a neutral capital on the edge of the Soviet bloc, where intelligence officers from every side of the Cold War are unusually thick on the ground. He works on the stay-behind networks, the arms caches and sleeper cells laid down across Western Europe against a Soviet occupation that never comes, the program later gathered under the name Gladio. The specific operations are not in the open biographies. The record gives the posting and its dates and nothing else.
suggested_refs: The Scandinavian stay-behind networks of the early 1950s, later gathered under the name Gladio

stops.name: Rome, buying an election and calling it a choice
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1953-1958 (Britannica); month unrecorded and defaulted. The mechanics of the funding are corroborated by general histories of CIA support to the Italian Christian Democrats rather than by any document naming Colby.
stops.campa: Under State Department cover, Colby runs covert political action in a country whose Communist Party is the largest in Western Europe. Cash moves through intermediaries into the campaigns of the Christian Democrats; the object is to hold Italy inside the NATO line by paying for the result at the ballot box. It is his schooling in the form of operation he will run for the next twenty years: choose a faction, fund it, and let the outcome be reported as a national decision. He will do the same next in a country at war.
suggested_refs: CIA covert funding of the Italian Christian Democrats through the elections of the 1950s
sources: General histories of CIA covert funding in postwar Italy

segments.name: Saigon Station and the Far East Division

stops.name: Saigon, chief of station
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1959 as the year of the posting (Britannica), with the station chief appointment following within the tour; month unrecorded and defaulted.
stops.campa: Colby arrives in Saigon and becomes chief of station as Ngo Dinh Diem's war against the insurgency in the countryside intensifies. He builds the paramilitary and political-action networks that the later American counterinsurgency programs are built on. He works alongside a government whose repression of its Buddhist and other opposition he is afterward accused of having underestimated. The station he runs here is the seed of the far larger apparatus he will come back to command a decade on, under a different name and with an ambassador's rank.
suggested_refs: The CIA Saigon station under Colby, 1959-1962, seedbed of the later pacification apparatus

stops.name: Langley, Virginia, the Far East Division
stops.date_confidence: attested: deputy chief on his return in 1962, chief from 1963 (Encyclopedia.com: 'chief of the Far East Division from 1963 onward'; Wikipedia: 'Far East Division: 1962, deputy, then chief'). The two posts are routinely conflated in secondary writing. Month unrecorded and defaulted. Note that the site is in Virginia, not the District of Columbia, as several summaries state.
stops.campa: He returns to headquarters, now at Langley, as deputy chief of the Far East Division, and takes the division itself the following year. The programs under him include the secret war in Laos and the paramilitary buildup that becomes the institutional ancestor of Phoenix, and he runs them while the American commitment in Vietnam goes from advisers to combat divisions. He is now an administrator of other men's field operations rather than a field man.
suggested_refs: The CIA Far East Division under Colby, 1963-1967

stops.name: Vientiane, the war that is not admitted
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No source places Colby personally in Vientiane; the stop marks the station his division ran and the date is set in the middle of his Far East Division tenure. His authority over the Laos program is not in dispute in any source.
stops.campa: From Langley, Colby holds ultimate responsibility for a war the United States will not admit to: Hmong forces under Vang Pao, armed and paid out of the embassy in Vientiane, flying on an airline the agency owns, fighting Pathet Lao and North Vietnamese units across a country that is neutral by treaty. Whether he ever stands in this city is not established in any reachable biography. His authority over what is run from it has never been in dispute, and the secret war outlasts his tenure over it by a decade.
suggested_refs: The CIA station at Vientiane and the Hmong paramilitary program under Vang Pao
sources: General histories of CIA operations in Laos under the Far East Division

stops.name: Saigon, CORDS and the rank of ambassador
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1968 for both the CORDS appointment and the personal rank of ambassador (Encyclopedia.com: 'headed the controversial CORDS/Phoenix program as ambassador in 1968'); the research pool dated the rank to 1969. Month unrecorded and defaulted.
stops.campa: Colby comes back to Vietnam as deputy to Robert Komer and takes over CORDS within months, holding the personal rank of ambassador over every pacification program in the country. Under CORDS sits Phoenix, built to identify and neutralize the Viet Cong's civilian infrastructure. Clark Clifford had flown into the Independence Palace the year before on the mission to gather more flags, and the hamlet metrics Colby now files travel up the same chain that briefs Clifford's Wise Men in Washington when they turn against the war.
suggested_refs: CORDS headquarters, Saigon, and the Phoenix Program directorate under Colby, 1968-1971
sources: Special Forces Chapter 78, 'Ambassador William E. Colby'

stops.name: Capitol Hill, testifying on Phoenix while it is still running
stops.date_confidence: attested: House Government Operations subcommittee testimony, July 1971, within the hearing series on U.S. Assistance Programs in Vietnam; the day is not given and is defaulted. The research pool graded this event as reconstruction, which understated it. The quotation carried here is from a 1981 interview, not the testimony: the wording circulating as 1971 testimony is untraceable to any transcript.
stops.campa: Colby testifies on Phoenix while the program is still operating, and concedes a body count. In the same hearing series a former military intelligence officer calls Phoenix a sterile depersonalized murder program. Colby answers that the killing is overwhelmingly combat killing and the enterprise is intelligence work, and he offers numbers rather than denials: twenty thousand five hundred and eighty-seven dead between January 1968 and May 1971. He will defend the program in these terms for the remaining twenty-five years of his life.
stops.quote: Now, some 28,000 were captured as well in various kinds of capture. Military capture, police capture, all sorts of things. And, 20,000 of the names that we had collected we found were killed.
stops.quote_source: William Colby, 1981 interview for 'Vietnam: A Television History,' American Archive of Public Broadcasting, cpb-aacip-15-4746q1sk6s
suggested_refs: Hearings on U.S. Assistance Programs in Vietnam, 1971, in which Colby and K. Barton Osborn both testified on Phoenix
sources: American Archive of Public Broadcasting, cpb-aacip-15-4746q1sk6s

stops.name: Langley, executive director-comptroller
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1972 (Wikipedia; Britannica); month unrecorded and defaulted.
stops.campa: He returns to headquarters as executive director-comptroller, the third-ranking officer of the agency and the man who runs its budget and its internal machinery. It is the first job of his career with no station and no country attached to it. Watergate is opening in the newspapers, two of the burglars are former agency men, and the institution he now administers from the inside is about to be asked, for the first time in its twenty-five years, to say out loud what it has been doing.
suggested_refs: The office of executive director-comptroller of the CIA, third-ranking post in the agency

stops.name: Langley, Deputy Director for Operations
stops.date_confidence: attested: 2 March to 24 August 1973. The title is Deputy Director for Operations, head of the clandestine service; the research pool's 'Deputy Director of Central Intelligence for Operations' conflates it with the separate office of Deputy Director of Central Intelligence.
stops.campa: Colby is made Deputy Director for Operations, head of the clandestine service, under a new Director of Central Intelligence, James Schlesinger, sent to the agency by a president who does not trust it. He holds the post one hundred and seventy-five days. In that time the clandestine service is cut hard, and the question of what the agency has done outside its charter stops being a matter of institutional memory passed between men who were there and becomes a matter of written record with names attached.
suggested_refs: The CIA Directorate of Operations under Colby, March to August 1973

stops.name: Langley, the order that produces the Family Jewels
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1973 (Wikipedia, 'Family Jewels'); the day of the directive is not carried in the sources consulted and is defaulted.
stops.campa: Schlesinger orders every employee of the agency to report to him in writing any activity, current or past, that might have fallen outside the legal charter. The submissions come in for weeks. What they assemble runs to six hundred and ninety-three pages: assassination plots against foreign heads of state, mail opened, journalists and antiwar activists watched inside the United States, drugs administered to men who did not know they were taking them. Inside the building the file acquires a name of its own, the Family Jewels.
suggested_refs: The 693-page 'Family Jewels' compilation, CIA, 1973

stops.name: Langley, sworn in as Director of Central Intelligence
stops.date_confidence: attested: 4 September 1973. The venue of the swearing-in is not specified in the sources consulted; the pin marks the agency he took over.
stops.campa: Colby is sworn in as the tenth Director of Central Intelligence, and the six hundred and ninety-three pages pass into his hands. One week later, in Santiago, Augusto Pinochet's aircraft are over La Moneda and Salvador Allende is dead; the agency's long work against that government is among the things the pages describe, and among the things a Senate committee will one day make Colby account for under oath. He inherits an institution with a written confession already sitting in its own safe.
suggested_refs: The Family Jewels report as transmitted to Colby on his appointment as DCI

stops.name: Langley, the war the estimates ruled out
stops.date_confidence: attested: the war opened 6 October 1973. The stop is placed at headquarters rather than at the front, since the event in Colby's life is the failure of the estimate rather than the fighting.
stops.campa: Egyptian and Syrian forces cross into Sinai and the Golan on the holiest day of the Jewish calendar, and the American intelligence community, Colby's community now, has said it would not happen. The estimates were wrong. The warning did not go out. He is five weeks into the job. The first crisis of his directorship is not a scandal but a plain failure of the thing the agency exists to do, and it arrives while the president who appointed him is being destroyed by a different set of tapes.
suggested_refs: The intelligence community's pre-war estimates of October 1973 and the post-mortems that followed
sources: Standard histories of the 1973 intelligence failure

stops.name: Langley, the letter on good secrets and bad
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1974 (National Security Archive, NSAEBB362); the day is not given and is defaulted.
stops.campa: Under attack from his own clandestine service for what he is prepared to let out, Colby sets down in writing the distinction he intends to govern by. Not everything can be kept. Not everything should be. The formulation separates three kinds of secret and defends only one of them. He is answering the chief of the clandestine service. It is written ten months before the Church Committee sits and nine months before the New York Times prints the contents of the file.
stops.quote: There are some 'bad secrets' which are properly revealed by an aggressive press. There are some older 'non-secrets' which no longer need to be kept secret and which we should gradually surface, but there are some 'good secrets' which deserve greater protection than we have been able to give them, in part by reason of their association with 'secrets' of lesser importance.
stops.quote_source: Letter from William Colby, March 1974, quoted in 'CIA History of DCI William Colby,' National Security Archive Electronic Briefing Book No. 362
suggested_refs: The CIA's declassified in-house history of the Colby directorship, NSAEBB362
sources: National Security Archive, NSAEBB362, 'CIA History of DCI William Colby'

stops.name: New York, the Hersh story on the front page
stops.date_confidence: attested: 22 December 1974. The pin is the New York Times building at 229 West 43rd Street, the paper's address in 1974.
stops.campa: Seymour Hersh puts on the front page what the Family Jewels contain: two decades of illegal domestic operations, files kept on American citizens, surveillance of the antiwar movement inside the United States by an agency forbidden by statute to operate there at all. The story runs on a Sunday, three days before Christmas, and it is sourced from a document that was written to be read by one man in one office. Twenty-seven years of institutional privacy end on this page.
suggested_refs: Seymour Hersh, 'Huge C.I.A. Operation Reported in U.S. Against Antiwar Forces,' New York Times, 22 December 1974
sources: Commentary Magazine, 'The War Within the CIA'

stops.name: Langley, the resignation of James Angleton
stops.date_confidence: attested: within about forty-eight hours of the Hersh story (Commentary Magazine).
stops.campa: Within about forty-eight hours of the Hersh story, Colby announces the resignation of James Jesus Angleton, chief of counterintelligence for twenty years and the officer named in the report for the mail-opening program. Confirming a newspaper story would have been one thing. Removing the man is another, and the building reads it correctly: the director is not going to fight this from behind the wall. Angleton's departure is the first of the removals.
suggested_refs: The CIA counterintelligence staff under James Jesus Angleton, 1954-1974
sources: Commentary Magazine, 'The War Within the CIA'

stops.name: The White House, the Rockefeller Commission
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1975 for the establishment of the commission; the day given here is that of the executive order and is not separately corroborated in the research pool, which gave only the month.
stops.campa: President Ford establishes a commission under his vice president to investigate the agency's domestic activities, the first of three inquiries that year. The choice of Nelson Rockefeller to run it is read at once as an attempt to keep the investigation inside the executive branch and away from Congress. It does not hold. Within weeks the Senate has voted its own committee into being, with subpoena power and a chairman from Idaho who has no intention of being managed by anybody.
suggested_refs: The Rockefeller Commission on CIA Activities within the United States, 1975
sources: Standard secondary literature on the 1975 Year of Intelligence

stops.name: Langley, counting the disasters in threes
stops.date_confidence: attested: memorandum of 7 January 1975, FRUS 1969-1976, Vol. XXXVIII Part 2, Document 25. The words are Colby's as relayed by Richard Helms to Lawrence Eagleburger, secondhand within a primary document.
stops.campa: Richard Helms, Colby's predecessor and now ambassador in Tehran, relays to the State Department a conversation with the director. Colby is counting his disasters, and he intends to cooperate with the Justice Department inquiry into the Family Jewels, and he has set exactly one condition on that cooperation: he will not break the law and he will not lie in order to meet it. It is the entirety of his defense, and it will cost him the agency inside the year.
stops.quote: First I had Phoenix, then Watergate, and now this.
stops.quote_source: Colby's words relayed by Richard Helms to Lawrence Eagleburger, memorandum of 7 January 1975, FRUS 1969-1976, Vol. XXXVIII, Part 2, Document 25
suggested_refs: FRUS 1969-1976, Vol. XXXVIII Part 2, Document 25, on the Family Jewels crisis
sources: Foreign Relations of the United States, 1969-1976, Vol. XXXVIII Part 2, Document 25 (history.state.gov)

stops.name: Capitol Hill, the Church Committee is voted into being
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1975 for the committee's creation and for Colby's extensive testimony before it; the day given is that of the Senate resolution. The quotation carried here is from the FRUS memorandum of 7 January 1975, three weeks earlier, and is placed for what it decided rather than for where it was said.
stops.campa: The Senate creates a select committee to study governmental operations with respect to intelligence activities, eleven senators under Frank Church, and Colby decides how he will meet it. Other men in the building want him to stonewall, on the ground that an intelligence service which answers questions is not an intelligence service. He goes in with the documents instead. Over the year he will disclose the assassination plots, the mind-control program, the mail opening, and the domestic surveillance, and be hated inside his own agency for it.
stops.quote: Yes, but I will not do anything illegal or lie in order to do so.
stops.quote_source: Colby's reply on cooperating with the Justice Department, relayed by Richard Helms to Lawrence Eagleburger, memorandum of 7 January 1975, FRUS 1969-1976, Vol. XXXVIII, Part 2, Document 25
suggested_refs: The Senate Select Committee to Study Governmental Operations with Respect to Intelligence Activities, 1975-1976
sources: Brookings Institution, '40 years ago, Church Committee investigated Americans spying on Americans'

stops.name: Independence Palace, Saigon, the war ends without him
stops.date_confidence: attested: 30 April 1975. The pin is the atlas's canonical Independence Palace coordinate, inherited from the Clifford file.
stops.campa: North Vietnamese armor comes through the gates of the palace, in the city where Colby ran the station in 1959 and the pacification of the whole country in 1968. Every structure he built there, the networks, CORDS, Phoenix, the hamlet metrics, ends on this morning in a state that no longer exists. He is in Washington, five months from being fired, testifying about an entirely different set of failures. The war he spent sixteen years inside closes while he is explaining the agency's past to the Senate.
suggested_refs: Independence Palace, Saigon, 30 April 1975

stops.name: Capitol Hill, the shellfish toxin on the committee table
stops.date_confidence: attested: 16 September 1975 (Church Committee hearing records; Brookings).
stops.campa: Colby brings to the committee table a quantity of shellfish toxin and cobra venom that the agency has kept for years in defiance of a presidential order to destroy it. The photographers get the dart pistol. The country gets the image of a sitting intelligence chief displaying his own service's contraband under oath. Inside the building it is the moment the case against him closes: not that he answered the questions, but that he brought the exhibits with him.
suggested_refs: Church Committee hearing of 16 September 1975 on the retained shellfish toxin and the dart pistol
sources: Brookings Institution, '40 years ago, Church Committee investigated Americans spying on Americans'

stops.name: The House side, refusing the Pike subpoena
stops.date_confidence: attested: statement by the Director of Central Intelligence, 29 September 1975 (National Security Archive, Document 29).
stops.campa: The House committee under Otis Pike runs harder than the Senate's and fights the agency over what it may publish, and Colby refuses a subpoena in writing rather than hand material across with no agreed procedure for its disclosure. The relationship never recovers. The full House will eventually vote against releasing Pike's final report at all. The man being called a traitor inside his own agency for cooperating with Congress is at the same moment defying a congressional committee in public over the same documents.
stops.quote: I cannot agree to the transfer of sensitive material in response to this subpoena in the absence of some agreed procedure as to its possible disclosure which I am still hopeful we can achieve.
stops.quote_source: Statement by Director of Central Intelligence William E. Colby, 29 September 1975, National Security Archive, Document 29
suggested_refs: The Pike Committee's suppressed final report and the subpoena dispute of September 1975
sources: General congressional intelligence-oversight histories of the Church and Pike Committees

stops.name: The White House, the Halloween Massacre
stops.date_confidence: attested: 3 November 1975. Not to be confused with the 1973 reduction of the clandestine service under Schlesinger, which some accounts also call a purge; the Halloween Massacre was a cabinet reshuffle done to Colby by the White House.
stops.campa: Ford reshuffles his entire national security team in a single stroke the press names the Halloween Massacre: Schlesinger out of the Pentagon, Kissinger stripped of one of his two hats, Colby told he is being replaced. He is offered an ambassadorial posting and declines it. The judgment behind the decision is that his candor before Congress cost the agency more than it bought, and it is delivered through the ordinary channels of a cabinet personnel change.
suggested_refs: The Ford cabinet reshuffle of 3 November 1975, known as the Halloween Massacre

stops.name: Langley, the last day and the handover
stops.date_confidence: attested: tenure ends 30 January 1976, George H. W. Bush sworn in the same day.
stops.campa: Colby's tenure ends after not quite two and a half years, and George H. W. Bush takes the seat, arriving at Langley in the year after the assassination plots and the mail openings were printed by the Senate. The files pass with the office. Manuel Noriega is still on the payroll. The Southern Cone network was founded in Santiago ten weeks before Colby's last day. Bush will hand the same inheritance on to William Casey. The chain of custody runs regardless of who is signing for it.
suggested_refs: The transfer of the Directorate of Central Intelligence from Colby to George H. W. Bush, 30 January 1976

stops.name: Washington, private practice and a late argument
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1977 for the founding of Colby, Miller and Hanes; month unrecorded and defaulted. The firm's street address is not in the reachable sources and the pin marks the downtown Washington legal district. The nuclear-freeze advocacy is attested only in summary form and is carried as reconstruction.
stops.campa: Out of office at fifty-six, Colby opens a Washington law firm under his own name and works as a security consultant, and in the years that follow becomes an unlikely public advocate of nuclear arms reduction and a nuclear freeze. Colleagues who remember who ran Phoenix find the late turn hard to place. He does not present it as a conversion. He argues it in the same register he used before the Senate: that power exercised without accounting to anybody eventually answers for nothing at all.
suggested_refs: Colby, Miller and Hanes, Washington, founded 1977

stops.name: New York, Honorable Men
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1978 for first publication by Simon and Schuster; no month is recorded and the day is defaulted. The pin is the publisher's Sixth Avenue address. The quotation is seen through a review's reproduction of the text and not against the original page image; the page number in circulation could not be confirmed.
stops.campa: Colby publishes his memoir, written with Peter Forbath, defending both the pacification of Vietnam and the disclosures to Congress as expressions of a single principle. The book sells, is reprinted in Britain and in paperback, and does not persuade the people it was written for. A second memoir, Lost Victory, will follow in 1989 to argue the Vietnam half of the case again. In the last pages of the first he concedes the distance between how he sees the agency and how the country does.
stops.quote: But I realize that my view of American intelligence and of its leading element the CIA, is much different from that of the ordinary citizen, and even from that of the well-informed minority.
stops.quote_source: William Colby, Honorable Men: My Life in the CIA (Simon and Schuster, 1978), quoted in Jeff Stein's review, archive.org item nsia-CIAColbyWilliamEHonorableMen
suggested_refs: Honorable Men: My Life in the CIA (1978) and Lost Victory (Contemporary Books, 1989)

stops.name: Rock Point, Maryland, last seen at a quarter past seven
stops.date_confidence: attested: about 7:15 p.m. on 27 April 1996 (Washington Post, 7 May 1996). Coordinates are the corrected position of Rock Point, 38 deg 16 min 19 sec N, 76 deg 50 min 27 sec W; figures circulating in the research pool put the place seventeen kilometers inland and off the river entirely.
stops.campa: Neighbors see him outside his weekend cottage at about a quarter past seven in the evening, on the Wicomico where it runs into the Potomac forty miles south of Washington. He has gone out alone in a canoe. He is seventy-six and twenty years out of the agency. The cottage is modest and the detail is domestic: the last known position of a man who spent thirty years arranging other people's disappearances, disappearing on an April evening with nothing arranged at all.
suggested_refs: Colby's weekend cottage at Rock Point, Charles County, Maryland
sources: Washington Post, 'Colby's Body Found Along River Shore,' 7 May 1996
Roanoke Times, 'Former CIA Chief's Body Found' (scholar.lib.vt.edu)

stops.name: The Wicomico River, the body on the marsh bank
stops.date_confidence: attested: canoe found beached 28 April, body recovered 6 May 1996, ruling issued 11 May. The length of the search is reported inconsistently: nine days from the last sighting on 27 April, eight from the finding of the canoe on 28 April. Both figures appear in the sources and neither is wrong.
stops.campa: The capsized canoe is found beached the morning after he was last seen. The body is not recovered for eight more days, face down on a marshy bank near the river's mouth. The medical examiner rules the death accidental: severe blockage of the left anterior descending artery, a cardiac or stroke event that put him over the side, then cold water and drowning. There is no evidence of any other hand. The ruling is issued and the rumors begin the same week, and thirty years later they have not stopped.
suggested_refs: Maryland Office of the Chief Medical Examiner findings on the death of William E. Colby, May 1996
sources: Washington Post, 'Colby's Body Found Along River Shore,' 7 May 1996
Deseret News, 11 May 1996, reporting the autopsy findings
HuffPost, 'Former CIA Director's Death Raises Questions, Divides Family'

stops.name: Arlington National Cemetery, Section 59, Grave 655
stops.date_confidence: attested: buried with military honors 13 May 1996, Section 59, Grave 655 (Arlington burial records; Find a Grave memorial 5898372). The absence of any monument elsewhere is an inference from a failed search plus the published criteria of the CIA Memorial Wall, and is carried as reconstruction.
stops.campa: He is buried with military honors in Section 59, Grave 655: a paratrooper who dropped twice into occupied Europe, a station chief, a director who told a Senate committee more than any of his predecessors had chosen to. His name is not on the memorial wall at Langley, which is reserved for officers killed in the line of duty, and an accidental drowning in retirement does not meet the standard. There is no statue anywhere and no building carries his name.
suggested_refs: Arlington National Cemetery, Section 59, Grave 655; and the CIA Memorial Wall criteria that exclude him

stops.name: New York, the son's film and the brother's answer
stops.date_confidence: attested: US release 23 September 2011 (First Run Features). The pin is the distributor's city; no premiere venue is specified in the sources. The quotation is from the 1978 memoir, placed here for what the family dispute is arguing about.
stops.campa: Fifteen years after the river, Colby's son Carl releases a documentary called The Man Nobody Knew and proposes that the drowning was a suicide, a man finally crushed by Vietnam and by Phoenix. His brother Jonathan rejects it flatly, calls their father a straightforward and unrepentant soldier, and points out that the body was found without shoes, which is what happens to a man kicking to stay afloat in cold water. The family cannot agree on how he died.
stops.quote: Their harsh opinion, in part, is, of course, the result of those questionable activities that have come to light and have cast a shadow of meanness, cynicism, and amorality over the intelligence profession.
stops.quote_source: William Colby, Honorable Men: My Life in the CIA (1978), quoted in Jeff Stein's review, archive.org item nsia-CIAColbyWilliamEHonorableMen
suggested_refs: The Man Nobody Knew: In Search of My Father, CIA Spymaster William Colby (dir. Carl Colby, First Run Features, 2011)
sources: HuffPost, 'Former CIA Director's Death Raises Questions, Divides Family'
